RESEARCH ARTICLE
Pilot-scale microaerobic hydrolysis-acidification and anoxic-oxic
processes for the treatment of petrochemical wastewater
Libing Chu1 & Pengyuan Ding2 & Mingcong Ding3
Received: 8 January 2021 /Accepted: 7 June 2021
# The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2021
Abstract
Microaerobic hydrolysis and acidification (MHA), as a promising pre-treatment method of industrial wastewater, is drawing
increasing attention to enhance the hydrolysis-acidification rate and inhibit the production of toxic gas H2S. In the present work, a
pilot-scale MHA reactor coupled with anoxic-oxic (A/O) processes for treating the petrochemical wastewater was established and
the mechanism and application of the MHA reaction were explored. The results showed that the ratio of VFA/COD was increased
by 43–90% and low effluent S2−concentration (less than 0.2 mg/L) was obtained after MHA treatment with 5.5–13.8 L air m−3
h−1 supply. The MHA sludge exhibited a good settleability, a higher protease activity and plentiful community diversity. In
addition to the dominant anaerobic bacteria responsible for hydrolysis and acidification such as Clostridiales uncultured,
Anaerovorax, Anaerolineaceae uncultured and Fastidiosipila, the sulfate reducing bacteria involving Desulfobacter,
Desulfomicrobium and Desulfobulbus, the sulphur oxidizing bacteria involving Thiobacillus, Arcobacter and Limnobacter,
the nitrifies such as Nitrosomonadaceae uncultured and Nitrospira, and denitrifies Thauera were also identified. MHA pre-
treatment guaranteed the efficacy and stability of the following A/O treatment. The removal efficiency of COD and ammonium of
the MHA-A/O system remained at around 78.3% and 80.8%, respectively, although the organic load fluctuated greatly in the
influent.
Keywords Microaeration . Biodegradation . Enzyme activity . Wastewater treatment . Bioreactors . Illumina sequencing
Introduction
The treatment of petrochemical wastewater produced from
petroleum refinery and manufacture of organic chemical ma-
terials such as ethylene, toluene, fiber, resins, plastics, and
pesticides, has become a challenging issue (Diya’uddeen
et al. 2011). Petrochemical wastewater contains many recalci-
trant hazardous pollutants involving aromatic hydrocarbons,
phenolics, heterocyclic compounds, aniline, etc. (Rubio-
Clemente et al. 2015). Therefore, the processes combined of
pre-treatment and secondary biological treatment are often
adopted to treat the refractory industrial wastewater (Guo
et al. 2014). The pre-treatment methods available include co-
agulation, chemical oxidation and hydrolysis, and acidifica-
tion (HA), etc. (Kakavandi and Babaei 2016; Lin et al. 2001;
Rubio-Clemente et al. 2015). Among them, HA pre-treatment
is promising owing to the fact that it was effective to improve
the biodegradability of wastewater. In addition, HA process
was economic and can withdraw the shock load (Ding et al.
2016; Wu et al. 2016).
Hydrolysis and acidification process is generally operated
at anaerobic conditions. Recently, studies have been more
concerned about the implementation of microaeration in the
anaerobic digestion system (Chen et al. 2020; JGdS et al.
2021; Loughrin et al. 2020; Ramos and Fdz-Polanco 2014;
Ruan et al. 2019). Microaeration hydrolysis and acidification
(MHA) is to dose small amounts of air into the HA reactor. It
was reported that the microaerobic condition contributed to
enhance the acidification degree, improve the biodegradability

of organic pollutants, and reduce H2S production in the bio-
gas, leading to odor-free effluent (Jenicek et al. 2008;
Krayzelova et al. 2015; Wu et al. 2018).
Lim et al. (2014) reported that with 5–7 mL O2 L−1 d−1
supply in the HA reactor treating brown water and food waste,
the levels of soluble COD and volatile fatty acids (VFA) in-
creased by 43.1–32.0% and 2.5–3.9%, respectively compared
to that under the anaerobic conditions. Chen et al. (2008)
found that the BOD5/COD ratio of pharmaceutical wastewater
increased from initial 0.20 to 0.36 by HA process under the
microaerobic condition, which was higher than that under the
anaerobic condition (0.30). Diaz et al. (2011) found that the
amount of H2S in the outflow biogas decreased dramatically
from 14.4 L m−3 by anaerobic digestion to below 0.3 L m−3 at
the microaeration conditions with 1.8 mL O2 min−1 supply
and elemental sulfur was the final product. Our previous lab-
scale studies showed that MHA was efficient to pre-treat the
mixture of petrochemical wastewater and domestic wastewa-
ter (Yang et al. 2015). The efficiency of COD removal was
33–42% in the MHA reactor and the ratio of BOD5/COD in
the MHA effluent reached 0.34.
In the present work, the pilot-scale MHA reactor was de-
veloped to pre-treat petrochemical wastewater. Studies were
focused on the microbial diversities and activities of sludge in
MHA reactor which were rarely considered in previous stud-
ies. In addition, the effect of microaeration intensity on
acidogenic degree and S2−production in MHA reactor was
assessed. The performance of MHA pre-treatment coupled
with anoxic/oxic (A/O) biological treatment processes was
evaluated in terms of organics and nutrients removal, compo-
sition of organic pollutants, and changes in the sludge mor-
phology. Taken together, this research would provide the use-
ful information about the mechanism of the MHA reaction
and contribute to the practical application of MHA-A/O sys-
tem in the treatment of industrial wastewater.
Materials and methods
Pilot-scale set-up
The pilot-scale MHA-A/O set-up was made of carbon steel
coated with fluoroplastic for corrosion protection. It was built
in a test workshop of a Petrochemical Wastewater Treatment
Plant (PWTP) located in a chemical industrial park of north-
east China. Figure 1 presents the diagram and picture of the
experiments set-up. The working volume of MHA and A/O
reactors was 14.5 m3 and 20.3 m3, respectively. The A/O
reactor is composed of 6 compartments, one served as anoxic
tank (A) and the other 5 compartment served as oxic tank
(O1–O5). There is an agitator in the anoxic tank to mix sludge
and wastewater. Air was introduced into the MHA reactor and
the oxic tanks through an air compressor and the flowrate was
controlled at 0.08–0.2 m3/h in the MHA tank and 8.0 m3/h in
the oxic tank by rotameters, respectively.
The raw petrochemical wastewater was settled in the pri-
mary setting tank and the supernatant was pumped into the
MHA reactor through a distribution reservoir. The effluent
from MHA tank after settlement entered into the A/O reactor
and the sludge settled was returned into the MHA reactor. The
effluent from A/O reactor entered into the secondary clarifier.
The supernatant was discharged into the sewer and sludge was
returned into the anoxic reactor with internal recycle ratio of
100%. A certain amount of excess sludge was withdrawn
from the secondary clarifier once a day to keep the sludge
retention time of 17–24 days.
Source and characteristics of petrochemical
wastewater
The raw petrochemical wastewater was derived from more
than 70 chemicals production plants in the chemical industrial
park. A variety of chemicals were made in the park including
ethylene, acrylate, isobutene, epoxy ethane, acrylonitrile bu-
tadiene styrene, vanillic aldehyde, fertilizers, pesticides,
resins, dyes, and refined oil, etc. Table 1 shows the character-
istics of the influent of MHA-A/O reactor. The influent COD
and ammonium fluctuated greatly which is typical for the
actual industrial wastewater. The soluble COD accounted for
89.2% in the total COD and a high level of sulfate were
observed.
Operational procedure of the pilot-scale MHA-A/O
system
The MHA and A/O reactors were inoculated with the return
sludge of the PWTP. The influent load was increased gradu-
ally by increasing the feeding rate according to the perfor-
mance of the bioreactors. When the COD removal reached
more than 15% in the MHA reactor and 70% in the A/O
reactor, the flowrate of influent was increased. The MHA-A/
O bioreactors were started up successfully after a month of
operation. Thereafter, the hydrolytic retention time was con-
trolled at 14 h and 20 h in the MHA and A/O reactor, respec-
tively. The levels of dissolved oxygen (DO) in MHA, anoxic
and oxic tank remained at 0.15–0.32 mg/L, 0.12–0.28 mg/L,
and 2.8–5.9 mg/L, respectively. The sludge retention time was
17–24 days. The oxidation reduction potential (ORP) ranged
from −240 to −360 mV in the MHA tank and from −102 to
−215 mV in the anoxic tank, respectively. The temperature
remained at 25–27 °C. The pH values in the influent and the
effluent from MHA, A and O tanks were 8.18, 7.74, 7.44, and
7.23, respectively. The inlet air flowrate in MHA tank was
controlled at 0.08–0.1 m3/h during the first 5 months of oper-
ation and increased to 0.2 m3/h in the last month to study the
impact of aeration intensity.

The samples of influent and effluent from MHA and sec-
ondary clarifier were taken periodically to detect the content
of COD, UV254, total nitrogen (TN), ammonium (NH4-N),
nitrate (NO3-N), nitrite (NO2-N) and total phosphorus (TP),
etc. The values of total suspended solids (TSS), volatile
suspended solids (VSS), SV (%) and SVI (mL g−1) of sludge
in the three tanks were monitored. For MHA reactor, the con-
centration of VFA, sulfate (SO4
2−) and sulfite (S2−) in the
influent and effluent was evaluated. The distribution of
COD, NH4-N, UV254, and NO3-N levels along the different
parts of the MHA-A/O bioreactors was evaluated at monthly
interval and the representative data were shown in the text. All
water samples were centrifuged at 9838 g for 5 min and the
supernatant obtained was collected for analysis.
When the operation of bioreactor reached steady state, the
composition of organic pollutants in the influent, MHA efflu-
ent and final effluent was assessed by GC-MS. The sludge
samples in the three tanks were taken to analyze the microbial
population and activity involving protease and dehydrogenase
activity. The microbial activity of biomass was closely related
to the substrates degradation rate. The activity of hydrolases
such as protease enables to reflect the microbial activity to
degrade the organic substrates (Gessesse et al. 2003).
Biological oxidation of the organic substances is a
dehydrogenation process and all living microorganisms have
a dehydrogenase activity, which is considered to be a sensitive
method for determining microbial activity (Lazarova and
Manem 1995).
Analytical methods
COD, nitrogen compounds, TP, sludge properties (TSS, VSS,
SV, and SVI) were evaluated according to the Standard
Methods (APHA/AWWA/AWEF 2017). VFA was detected
using titration method. UV254 was measured by a Lambda25
UV-Vis spectrophotometer (PerkinElmer, USA). pH was de-
tected using a pH meter (SX721, Shanxin, China). ORP and
DO concentrations were evaluated using a portable WTW
DO/ORP meter (multi 3420, Germany).
The identification of the organic pollutants was conducted
using Agilent GC-MS analyzer (7890A/5975C, USA)
equipped with OV-101 capillary column. Before GC-MS
analysis, the organic pollutants were extracted from the waste-
water samples using dichloromethane as the extraction re-
agent. The temperature of GC injection port was 280 °C and
the carrier gas was helium. The oven temperature program
was as follows: initializing to 55 °C for 4 min and raising to

280 °C with a step of 10 °C min−1. The ion source temperature
of MS detector was 200 °C.
The protease activity of sludge (U/g VSS) was determined
using 0.5% azocasein as chromogenic substrate (Kim et al.
2002). One unit of protease activity (1 U) represents to de-
grade 1 mg of azocasein at 37°C and reaction of 90 min. The
dehydrogenases activity of sludge was determined using
triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) as indicator (Tarjányi-
Szikora et al. 2013). TTC was reduced into red-colored
triphenyl formazan (TF) which can be quantified by spectrom-
etry. The dehydrogenases activity was expressed as mg TF/g
VSS.
The microbial community of sludge in different tanks was
analyzed by Illumina MiSeq sequencing (Yang et al. 2015).
DNA was extracted using OMEGA soil DNA extraction kit
(E.Z.N.A., USA) and examined using 1% agarose gel electro-
phoresis. The specific primers 338F (ACTCCTACGGGAGG
CAGCA) and 806R (GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT)
with barcode was designed and synthesized. The PCR reac-
tion was carried out in solution of 20 μL involving 5×FastPfu
Buffer 4 μL, forward primer 0.8 μL, reverse primer 0.8 μL,
template DNA 10 ng, dNTPs 2 μL, FastPfu Polymerase 0.4
μL and ddH2O. Thermal cycling included 1× (3 min at 95°C),
27× (30 s at 95°C, 30 s at 55 °C, 45 s at 72°C), 1× (10 min at
72°C) and 10°C until halted by user. Then, the PCR products
were examined by 2% agarose gel electrophoresis, purified
using the AxyPrep DNA Gel Extraction Kit according to man-
ufacturer’s protocols and quantified using Quantus™
Fluorometer (Promega, USA). Finally, the purified amplicons
were pooled in equimolar and paired-end sequenced on an
Illumina MiSeq PE300 platform according to the standard
protocols by Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co. Ltd.
(Shanghai, China). The raw 16S rRNA gene sequencing reads
were demultiplexed, quality-filtered by fastp version 0.20.0
and merged by FLASH version 1.2.7. The average length of
the bases was 441 bp. The clustering and taxonomy analysis
of Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) was conducted at a
similarity level of 97% using UPARSE version 7.1. Chimeric
sequences were identified and removed. The taxonomy of
each OTU representative sequence was analyzed by RDP
Classifier version 2.2 against the 16S rRNA database (e.g.
Silva v138) using confidence threshold of 0.7.
Results and discussion
Organics and nutrients removal
After start-up, the pilot-scale MHA-A/O bioreactor was oper-
ated continually for 6 months, except for the period from 22nd
to 30th day when the feeding of the bioreactor was stopped
owing to the shut-down of the PWTP for maintenance.
Figure 2 depicts the variation of COD and NH4-N
concentrations in influent and effluent as well as the efficiency
of COD and NH4-N removal. Although COD concentration in
the influent fluctuated greatly, it remained at 98.9 ± 27.5 mg/L
in the final effluent. The COD removal of the overall system
ranged 70–87% with the average of 78.3%, while around 20%
of COD reduction was achieved in MHA reactor. Similar
results were reported by other researchers. Song et al. (2019)
studied the treatment of 2-butenal manufacture wastewater by
MHA process. Results showed that around 23.7% of COD
removal was obtained and the acidification degree could reach
20.9%.
The efficiency of NH4-N removal was higher than that of
COD removal except for some periods when the influent
NH4-N concentration was much high (up to 80 mg/L). The
efficiency of NH4-N removal reached 80.8 ± 15.7% and a low
level of 5.9 ± 2.9 mg NH4-N/L was observed in the final
effluent. This demonstrates that the activity of nitrifying bac-
teria was high in the A/O reactor. The NH4-N concentration
increased after MHA treatment owing to ammonification.

This could also suggest that the activity of ammonifying bac-
teria was not affected under the microaerobic conditions, lead-
ing to the conversation of organic nitrogen to ammonium.
Some nitrogen-containing organic pollutants such as pyridine,
aminobenzene and acetochlor etc. were identified in the raw
petrochemical wastewater according to GC-MS results (as
shown in the following Fig. 4). The effluent TN concentration
maintained at 16.9 ± 5.0 mg/L and the TN removal was
around 47.3%. The TP level in the effluent was 0.43 ± 0.47
mg/L and around 64.3% of TP removal was achieved by
MHA-A/O treatment.
Figure 3 presents the alteration of COD, NH4-N, UV254
and NO3-N levels along the different part from inlet to outlet
of the system. The NO2-N concentration in the effluent was
very low (0.04 ± 0.02 mg/L). This suggested that nitrification
in A/O reactor took place completely. As shown in Fig. 3,
each part of the system contributed to the removal of COD
and UV254, while the degradation occurred mainly in the A/O
reactor. The absorbance of UV254 was eliminated by 18%
after MHA treatment and more than 60% after A/O treatment.
This suggests that the aromatic compounds having C=C and
C=O double bonds were removed mainly in A/O reactors.
After MHA pre-treatment, the macro-molecular and recalci-
trant pollutants are converted into the micro-molecular and
less toxic substances which were then transformed into the
volatile organic acid such as acetate and butyric acid (Wang
et al. 2014). Those substances could be degraded easily into
CO2 and water by the following A/O biological treatment.
The performance of the pilot-scale MHA-A/O system was
comparable to that of the bench-scale bioreactor reported in
our previous studies. The effluent COD values were similar
and NH4-N concentration was lower in the bench-scale sys-
tem. Around 99 mg COD/L and 1.3 mg NH4-N/L were ob-
tained in the effluent of the bench-scale MHA-A/O bioreac-
tors (Ding et al. 2016; Yang et al. 2015). It should be noted
that the feeding wastewater of the bench-scale system was
composed of petrochemical wastewater and domestic waste-
water (3:1). In the present pilot-scale MHA-A/O system, the
wastewater was totally from the petrochemical industry. The
Environmental Protection Agency of China has published a
new strict emission standard of pollutants in petrochemical
wastewater (GB 31571-2015). The permissible discharge lev-
el of COD declined from 100 mg/L in the old standard
(GB8978-1996) to 60 mg/L. The new standard for
discharging NH4-N, TN, and TP was 8.0 mg/L, 40 mg/L,
and 1.0 mg /L, respectively. The results showed that the
NH4-N, TN, and TP concentrations in the effluent from the
pilot-scale MHA-A/O bioreactor have met the new discharge
standard, but the COD content was higher. The advanced
treatment processes after MHA-A/O bioreactor seem to be
necessary to attain COD limit.

acidification degree and H2S production in MHA reactor.
The efficiency of acidogenic fermentation was high within
the microaeration intensity applied. The ratio of VFA/COD
in the MHA effluent was increased by 43% with the aeration
intensity of 5.5–6.9 L air m−3 h−1 and by 90% with 13.8 L air

Characterization of organic pollutants
As shown in Fig. 4, a variety of organic compounds including
methacrylate, pyridine, chlorobenzene, styrene,
aminobenzene, acetophenone, naphthalene, acetochlor, etc.
were identified in the raw petrochemical wastewater. Those
compounds are the raw materials/intermediates/monomers to
produce plasticizer, dyes, resin, pesticide, etc. After MHA
treatment, almost a half of pollutants disappeared, while only
two compounds were detected and their abundance was de-
clined remarkably after A/O treatment. This indicates the ef-
fectiveness of MHA-A/O treatment in decomposition of the
toxic organic pollutants. In the new standard (GB 31571-
2015), the discharge limits to more than 60 pollutants involv-
ing bisphenol A (0.1 mg/L), polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon
(0.02 mg/L), acrylonitrile (2.0 mg/L), styrene (0.2 mg/L) and
aminobenzene (0.5 mg/L) were required. The results of GC-
MS analysis demonstrated that the MHA-A/O processes were
promising to treat petrochemical wastewater to meet the new
requirement in discharging the organic pollutants.
Alternation of sludge concentration and property
Figure 5 reveals the changes in sludge concentration, the ratio
of VSS/TSS, SV and SVI indices in MHA, A and O tanks
during the half a year of operation. The TSS concentrations in
the MHA tank fluctuated in the ranges of 2.8–6.5 g/L, which
might be attributed to the effect of the microaeration on sludge
retention. The microaeration operation should be controlled
carefully to prevent the sludge washout. The ratio of VSS/
TSS of MHA sludge decreased from 64% to 48%, which
indicated that the accumulation of the inorganic substances
occurred in the MHA tank. However, the pre-treatment of
MHA guaranteed the efficacy of A/O reactor. The sludge con-
centration increased gradually in the anoxic and oxic tanks
and ratio of VSS/TSS remained at a high level of around
70%, which is consisted with the high degradation efficiency
of A/O reactor. It is noted that the introduction of limited
oxygen did not affect the settleability of sludge. SV and SVI
of sludge in the three tanks maintained at relatively low levels

Microbial activity and community
Figure 6 presents the activities of protease and dehydroge-
nases of the sludge in MHA, anoxic and oxic tanks. The
MHA sludge exhibited a higher protease activity than the A/
O sludge, whereas the dehydrogenases activity was higher for
the sludge in the A and O tanks. The results of enzymes ac-
tivity were consistent with the function in each tank. The
higher protease activity of the biomass facilitated to improve
the hydrolysis rate of the macro-molecular substances in the
petrochemical wastewater. The organic pollutants were oxi-
dized into CO2 and water mainly by the A/O treatment corre-
sponding to the higher dehydrogenase activity.
The Illumina MiSeq sequencing obtained 22,375 se-
quences for each sludge sample with high Good’s coverage
of more than 99%. The MHA sludge had the highest commu-
nity richness and diversity with Ace and Simpson indices of
941 and 0.0156, following by the oxic sludge (Ace index 906
and Simpson index 0.0153) and anoxic sludge (Ace index 899
and Simpson index 0.0304). Figure 7 reveals the taxonomic
composition of sludge in the three tanks. The sludge in the A
and O tank has a higher similarity. At the phylum levels,
Proteobacteria and Firmicutes were predominant in MHA
sludge, while Proteobacteria and Bacteroidetes were highly
enriched in A and O sludge. Similar results were observed by
other studies. Lim et al. reported that more diverse bacteria
community was detected in the MHA reactor (18 OTUs affil-
iated to 4 phyla), whereas only 7 bacterial OTUs (affiliated to
2 phyla) were identified in the anaerobic reactor (2014).

organics were more abundant in MHA reactor, leading to a
higher hydrolysis efficiency. Proteobacteria is the largest
phylum of bacteria and includes broad variety of members
of degrading organic pollutants degradation and denitrifica-
tion (Snaidr et al. 1997). Bacteroidetes are commonly identi-
fied in fermentation and acidification bioreactors serving to
decompose the macromolecular substances such as cellulose,
fiber, starch, and protein (Nakasaki et al. 2009).
The heatmap generated from the major genera in sludge
samples was shown in Fig. 8. Bacteria belonging to
Clostridiales uncultured, Christensenellaceae uncultured,
Gemmatimonadaceae uncultured, Thauera, Fastidiosipila,
Betaproteobacteria unclassified and Anaerovorax were dom-
inant in MHA bioreactor. The members enriched highly in A/
O bioreactor include Thauera, Gemmatimonadaceae uncul-
tured, Nitrosomonadaceae uncultured, Ferruginibacter,
Thiobacillus, Comamonadaceae unclassified,
Betaproteobacteria unclassified and Blastocatella. Among
them, Blastocatella is especially highly enriched in the oxic
tank. Five clusters were involved from cluster analysis.
The microbial community distribution in different tanks
determines its functionality. The higher abundance of genera
Clostridiales uncultured, Christensenellaceae uncultured
(21%) belonging to class Clostridium was observed in MHA
reactor. Bacteria affiliated to Clostridium are reported to be
the acidogenic populations, which are able to utilize carbohy-
drates to generate H2 and VFAs (Chu et al. 2012). The com-
munity Clostridium was reported to be predominant in dark
fermentative H2-producing bioreactor (Im et al. 2012). The
members of genus Gemmatimonadaceae were detected in
the activated sludge processes for sewage treatment under
both anaerobic and aerobic conditions (Xu et al. 2017). The
genus Fastidiosipila was identified in the anaerobic
biomethanization consortium of municipal solid waste
(Bertin et al. 2012). A strain of Fastidiosipila was report to
grow under both anaerobic conditions and the presence of 2%
and 6% O2 (Falsen et al. 2005). The strains of Anaerovorax
were found to be strictly anaerobic, which could ferment pu-
trescine to acetate, butyrate, H2 and ammonium (Matthies
et al. 2000).
Some strains belonging to genus Blastocateewalla were
aerobic chemoorganotrophic organisms and isolated from
the soil (Foesel et al. 2013). The members of genus
Ferruginibacter were reported to be Gram-negative, strictly
aerobic rods and isolated from wetland freshwater (Kang et al.
2015). The higher abundance of Nitrosomonadaceae was
consisted with the good nitrification in A/O reactor. The mem-
bers of Thauera (Morgan-Sagastume et al. 2008),
Thiobacillus (Li et al. 2016), Comamonadaceae and
Betaproteobacteria (Wang and Chu 2016) were reported to
have the function of denitrification. In addition, the bacteria
having high abundance in the MHA and A/O system include
glycogen-accumulating organisms Defluviicoccus for
enhanced phosphorus removal (Burow et al. 2007), phenol-
degrading bacterium Ottowia (Cao et al. 2014), semi-
syntrophic fatty acids-oxidizing bacteria Anaerolineae
(Narihiro et al. 2012) and sulfur oxidizing bacterium
Limnobacter (Chen et al. 2016).
It is clear that the sludge in the MHA reactor exhibited a
plentiful community diversity. In addition to the dominant
bacteria responsible for hydrolysis and acidification such as
Clostridiales, Anaerovorax, Anaerolineaceae uncultured and
Fastidiosipila (total abundance 35%), the aerobic nitrifiers
such as Nitrosomonadaceae uncultured and Nitrospira were
identified with a relatively high abundance (1.3% and 3.3%
respectively). This might explain the increased nitrate concen-
tration in MHA effluent (Fig. 3). The denitrifying bacteria
Thauera was also found in MHA sludge with high abundance
(6.4%). It is also noted that there were co-existed the sulfate
reducing bacteria (SRB) such as Desulfobacter,
Desulfomicrobium and Desulfobulbus, etc. (total abundance
4.2%) and the sulphur oxidizing bacteria (SOB) such as

Thiobacillus Arcobacter and Limnobacter (total abundance
2.8%) in the MHA bioreactor. Generally, SRB are considered
to be obligate anaerobes. Recent studies found that SRB were
able to survive in the presence of limited oxygen (Ontiveros-
Valencia et al. 2014). The studies by Jenicek et al. (2011)
demonstrated that the activity of SOB in the microaerobic
sludge (10.4 mg/g h) was significantly higher in comparison
with the anaerobic sludge (6.1 mg/g h), while the activity of
SRB was not affected with limited air supply of 2.0 mg/g h.
Wu et al. (2015) documented that SRB occupied for 2.8% in
the lab-scale anaerobic HA reactor and their abundance
dropped to 0.9% under microaerobic conditions.
Conclusions
The results of the pilot-scale study indicated that MHA pre-
treatment coupled with A/O bioreactor was promising in
treating petrochemical wastewater. MHA pre-treatment en-
sured the efficacy and stability of the following A/O treat-
ment. Although the influent fluctuated, the efficiency of
COD and NH4-N removal maintained at around 78.3% and
80.8%, respectively. Nearly half of organic pollutants disap-
peared after MHA treatment, and only two compounds were
detected and their abundance declined greatly after A/O treat-
ment. The ratio of VFA/COD increased by 43–90% in the
MHA effluent and the S2−concentration (0.2 mg/L) was low
with 5.5–13.8 L−air m−3 h−1.
The MHA sludge exhibited the higher protease activity,
whereas the dehydrogenases activity was higher for the sludge
in A/O tanks. Illumina MiSeq sequencing showed that the
MHA sludge had the highest community richness and diver-
sity and the predominant genera were Clostridiales
uncultured, Gemmatimonadaceae uncultured,
Christensenellaceae uncultured, Thauera, Fastidiosipila,
Betaproteobacteria unclassified and Anaerovorax. In addition
to the dominant bacteria responsible for hydrolysis and acid-
ification, SRB, SOB, ammonium-oxidizing bacteria, nitrite-
oxidizing bacteria and denitrifies were coexisted in MHA
reactor.
